19693-fighting-for-peace:
Samuel Kinkade Cowan titled his book Fighting for Peace, a phrase that carries its own argument. The pairing was much debated after the First World War. Many writers then asked how war could serve peace. The copy preserved here wanders into a gazetteer entry on Potsdam, the Prussian court city near Berlin. That entry notes Potsdam lost its second-capital status in 1918.

Scraps like that show how war books were assembled from mixed stock. Memoir, argument, and reference matter often shared one binding. The title alone marks the book's era. After 1918, every peace plan had to answer the trenches. Cowan's title states the paradox those plans had to solve.
19709-danger-in-deep-space:
Danger in Deep Space is a young readers' space adventure in the Solar Guard setting. It opens with an order to cut thrust on the main drive rockets. A tall officer in Solar Guard uniform watches the telescanner screen. Earth grows larger across the Western Hemisphere view. The cadets of the Solar Guard face trouble far from home.

Space cadet stories taught science through cliff-hangers. Rockets, scanners, and ranks gave young readers a future navy in space. Each chapter ended on danger, as serial fiction must. This volume belongs to the Tom Corbett style of space patrol tales. It shows how the 1950s sold the space age to boys. The optimism is as period-true as the rockets.
19872-three-french-moralists-and-the-gal:
Three French Moralists and the Gallantry of France studies French character through its classic moralists. Edmund Gosse wrote it during the Great War. He takes a wartime utterance almost at random as a test. It distinguishes the Frenchman's attitude in violent action, he says. Other races are equally brave and effective, he grants. The French manner, though, has its own gallantry. Montaigne's heirs stand behind that manner.

France's moralists, La Rochefoucauld chief among them, anatomized motive and honor. Gosse, a man of letters, links their tradition to soldiers of 1914. The book is criticism serving an alliance. It tells British readers why France fights as she does. Elegant and slight, it is a wartime essay with real learning.
20066-ethics-in-service:
William Howard Taft published Ethics in Service in 1915, a set of talks on public duty. Taft had served as president and knew public life from the top. He warns against the claim that we can learn nothing from the past. Some act as if new plans could make men wholly new at once.

Taft argues that human motives stay much the same across time. Good service, then, rests on old virtues used with care. The book speaks to officials, lawyers, and citizens alike. Readers get a calm, firm case for duty, law, and steady character in public work.
20072-with-the-colors-songs-of-the-ameri:
Everard Jack Appleton published With the Colors in 1917, songs of the American service. The poems speak of the flag in plain, strong words. It is not just for show, one verse insists at the start. To those who follow it, the flag means their country, right or wrong.

Appleton wrote for troops entering the First World War. His verses aim to lift hearts and stiffen resolve in camp and field. The book holds march songs, tributes, and tales in rhyme. Readers get a sense of how Americans in 1917 sang about duty, home, and the flag they served.
20084-the-beach-of-dreams-a-romance:
H. De Vere Stacpoole wrote The Beach of Dreams, a romance of the sea. Raft, a big red-haired sailor, has used the sea since age twelve. At thirty-two, he has twenty years of ships and storms behind him. His past blurs into fo'c'sles, bar-rooms, and blazing suns.

Stacpoole knew ships and far ports, and his tales breathe salt air. On some beach of dreams, such men seek rest, love, or gold. The sea gives and takes in equal measure in his work. Readers get romance shaped by real sailor life, rough edges and all.
20156-strife-and-peace:
Strife and Peace is a novel set amid the grand mountains of Norway. A huge chain runs out toward Romsdahlshorn, whose foot meets the Atlantic. Southward it takes names like Langfjeld, Sognefjeld, Filefjeld, and Hardangerfjeld. For a hundred and fifty miles, nature shows all her grandeur there.

Such a stage suits a tale of hearts in conflict and calm. Strife and peace, as the title promises, rule lives as well as lands. Fjords, farms, and fierce weather shape the people on the page. Readers get Scandinavian romance with the land itself as a lead presence.
20192-orrain-a-romance:
S. Levett-Yeats published Orrain, a romance, in 1904, set in old France. The narrator's great-uncle, the Bishop of Seez, shapes his early fate. At that bishop's urging, his mother sends him to become a churchman. At seventeen, he is packed off to the College of Cambrai in Paris.

A church career chosen by others sets up a life of conflict. Levett-Yeats wrote tales of India and Europe with a soldier's eye. Old France gives this romance duels, courts, and faith under strain. Readers get historical romance told by a hero caught between callings.
20194-the-petticoat-commando-boer-women-:
Johanna Brandt wrote The Petticoat Commando, on Boer women in secret service. On October 11, 1899, martial law was declared across two Boer republics. The Transvaal and Orange Free State braced as British subjects fled. In Pretoria, Boers and their friends stayed to face the coming war.

For eight months, they enjoyed Boer freedom under Boer martial law. Brandt tells how women passed news, hid men, and aided the cause. Her account comes from inside that tense, watched capital city. Readers get a rare woman's view of the Boer War's hidden front.
20257-a-political-romance:
Laurence Sterne wrote A Political Romance, a sharp satire of church politics in York. Master Trim has set his heart on an old watch-coat in church. It has hung there for many years, unused and forgotten by most. Trim wants it made into a warm petticoat and a jerkin.

He begs his reverence, in a plaintive tone, to consent to the plan. Behind that small plea sit feuds over posts, pride, and petty power. Sterne, author of Tristram Shandy, turns a coat into a comic weapon. Readers get brief, biting satire from one of English prose's great wits.
20296-the-stranger-in-france:
The Stranger in France holds sketches taken on the spot during a trip there. The writer penned them at first for private reading by close friends. At their urging, he now offers them to the public eye. He names William Hayley among the friends he is proud to list.

Such travel sketches prize fresh scenes over deep research or plans. Markets, roads, inns, and manners fill the pages in quick strokes. Trips to France after war years drew keen English interest then. Readers get an early, lively set of French impressions from an English guest.
20445-the-coast-of-chance:
The Coast of Chance is a novel of fashionable life, where wealth and glitter set the stage. Its heroine pauses before a mirror and studies her own reflection. For a moment she sees herself only as a figure in the foreground of a picture.

Through that open door, the room beyond shines with a bright, hard glitter. The image sets the book's tone: beautiful surfaces, sharp light, and feelings kept under polish. The story follows its heroine along the risky coast where chance, love, and social standing meet, in a world that watches every move.
20523-religion-and-art-in-ancient-greece:
Ernest A. Gardner's Religion and Art in Ancient Greece studies how Greek faith shaped Greek art. Gardner taught archaeology and knew the temples and statues at first hand. The book asks what worshippers believed their gods' images really were.

The better educated, Gardner writes, would regard the images as symbolic aids. They helped focus the force of religious ideas and hopes. But among common people, the images tended to be taken for much more. That gap between symbol and idol, he shows, runs through the whole story of Greek art and worship.
20566-rogers-isms-the-cowboy-philosopher:
Will Rogers published Rogers-Isms in 1919, billed as the cowboy philosopher on the peace conference. Rogers had gone to Paris where the Great War's peace was being made. He reported back in the Oklahoma drawl and rope-trick humor that made him America's favorite wit.

His jokes land on high and low alike. They say the most perfect English in this country is spoken in Sing Sing, he writes, and at the federal prison in Atlanta. They claim a knife never touched a lip there. You can see, he adds, where that junk leads you. The book mixes manners, politics, and nonsense.
20659-ministry-of-disturbance:
Ministry of Disturbance is a science fiction story of a far-future emperor and his robot court. The ruler sits in a palace where machines wait on every wish. He notices that the robot is still beside his chair, waiting for dismissal, though the audience has ended.

He orders it to summon the cleaning robots and sends it away. He could as easily have summoned them himself, or let the guards who would be in checking the rooms. The story uses that idle, absolute power to ask what an emperor is for, in a tale of revolt inside a perfect palace.
20662-the-measurement-of-intelligence:
Lewis M. Terman's The Measurement of Intelligence explains the Binet-Simon intelligence scale and its American revision, the Stanford-Binet. Terman, a Stanford psychologist, turned the French tests into standard American practice. The book lays out the scale's nature, its making, and its special character.

Its method rests on age standards. Children are tested against what most children of their age can do, across the kinds of mental functions the scale calls into play. Binet, Terman notes, would test general intelligence itself. The book founded an industry of testing, with effects on schools that are argued about still.
20764-the-death-of-saul-and-other-eisted:
Prize poems from Welsh contests fill The Death of Saul and its companion pieces. One verse urges the bard not to fear sharp critics. Grass grows strong where mowers wound it, the poem says, and so does the poet.

The eisteddfod, Wales's famed contest of song and verse, shaped this book. Bible tales, hymns, and Welsh pride meet in its pages. Saul's fall gives the lead poem a grave, grand theme. English verse here carries a Welsh heart, with music and moral weight in each piece. Readers meet a culture that crowned its poets in public contest.
20796-the-colors-of-space:
Earth stuns young Bart in The Colors of Space, a 1963 tale of star travel. He first saw Earth at age twelve, thrilled to reach mankind's old home world. The first sight that met him off the starship was the Lhari spaceport.

Marion Zimmer Bradley wrote this tale of a human youth among alien Lhari. Bart must pass in a world where men are few and suspect. Mistrust, hidden plans, and first contact strains drive the plot. The book shows early Bradley at work on themes she later made famed: outsiders, identity, and the cost of belonging among strangers.
20803-the-war-of-independence:
Old textbooks, says John Fiske, never asked why men stood where they stood at Yorktown. They missed the living questions behind the War of Independence. Big histories, he adds, bury key facts in a sea of small ones.

Fiske wrote American history that plain readers could grasp and enjoy. His War of Independence sorts the cardinal facts from the minor ones with care. Causes, campaigns, and the birth of a nation take clear shape. The book reflects his gift: deep study told in brisk, lucid prose that made history a popular subject in his day.
20869-the-skylark-of-space:
Praise calls The Skylark of Space one of the great space flight tales for years to come. Love and romance weave through its science, the notices stress. E. E. Smith wrote it with Lee Hawkins Garby in the pulp dawn.

A chance lab find gives Richard Seaton a drive that leaps the stars. Foes chase his Skylark for the secret of its vast power. Smith's first novel launched the space opera age in earnest. Readers still come to it for sheer scale: worlds, fleets, and wonders piled high at breakneck speed, with heart beneath the roar.
20988-islands-of-space:
John W. Campbell took the helm of Astounding Stories in 1937 and raised science fiction's bar. Islands of Space, his own tale from 1956 in book form, shows the hand that did it. Moreau, Fuller, and a faster-than-light drive star in its pages.

Arcot's crew leaps between island universes in a ship of wild power. Black suns, alien worlds, and space battles crowd their vast tour. Campbell wrote bold, idea-rich tales before he turned famed editor. This one keeps his early fire: big physics, brave crews, and the thrill of a cosmos far larger than men had dared dream.
20995-fighting-in-france:
Earl and Leon Platt, two American boys in French khaki, rest behind the lines in Champagne. Ross Kay opens Fighting in France, from 1916, in a province already scarred by heavy war. The Big War, as all then called it, frames their service.

Kay's Fighting series followed American lads through the Great War's fronts. Trenches, raids, gas, and guns fill this French volume's brisk chapters. The Platt boys serve before America joins the war in full. Such tales let home readers track the conflict through young eyes, keen, scared, and proud by turns on foreign soil.
21086-the-penang-pirate-and-the-lost-pin:
John Conroy Hutcheson pairs two shorter sea tales in one volume. In the first, the captain of the Hankow Lin suspects pirates will attack his ship on the return voyage from Canton to Australia. He lays plans to spoil their fun, and the pirate schooner is beaten when it strikes.

The second tale follows a pinnace from HMS London, left behind off the East African coast during a hunt for slave dhows. A storm drives the boat toward Madagascar, and some of the crew are lost. The bosun, who tells the story years later in England, brings the rest ashore.
21547-the-gap-in-the-fence:
Frederica J. Turle sets The Gap in the Fence at Haver Grange, in a 1914 Sunday School Union tale. The empty Grange, long marked to let furnished, draws the local children in. They treat its mossy walks and weedy beds as their own special ground.

A queer visitor, then a little foreign girl, breaks the quiet of the place. Chapters move through fairies, gypsies on the common, and Una's pet and questions. Watson Charlton's twelve pictures show the cast, from Ruth to Tom. Sad days and a father's secret close a gentle tale of village children and their finds.
21557-newton-forster-or-the-merchant-ser:
Newton Forster serves in merchant ships, not the Royal Navy, in Captain Marryat's novel of 1832. It was Marryat's third book and his first with a merchant hero. A preface growls at kind friends whose unsought remarks cut deeper than any critic's.

Marryat knew both services, and he shows the merchantman's risks as keenly as the warship's. Trade voyages, press gangs, wrecks, and love ashore shape Newton's rise. The tale argues that courage and skill are not the navy's alone. Its two volumes move fast, in the full early Marryat manner, with storms, chases, and hard bargains throughout.
21698-rivers-of-ice:
R. M. Ballantyne brings a bluff sailor home in Rivers of Ice, opening near London Bridge at mid-century. The man looks under forty though past fifty, with a saltwater face and shaggy black hair. A huge beard and broad hat hint at the diggings and the backwoods.

A street boy nearby strikes a pose, lips pursed like a rosebud in a dirty bush. Ballantyne's eye for such figures fills the tale with London colour. The rover's return draws old shipmates and new dangers together. Glaciers give the book its title, but its heart lies in the sailor's search for home and kin.
21709-the-walrus-hunters-a-romance-of-th:
Written in 1893, near the end of R. M. Ballantyne's life, this northern tale brings two peoples together in the ice country. A Dogrib band and an Eskimo band start as wary foes, as was common between their peoples. In the course of the story, members of the two groups become close friends and work toward a shared goal.

The editor of this edition calls it one of Ballantyne's very best books, full of action from start to finish. Hunting, travel, and hard weather in the far north fill the pages. Readers also come away knowing more about how both peoples lived, hunted, and saw the world around them.
21711-the-world-of-ice:
Old sailor John Buzzby stands at the heart of this Arctic whaling tale by R. M. Ballantyne. Buzzby is a true-blue tar of the old school, first awake each morning and last asleep each night. The opening chapters look back over his long life at sea, his fights, and the strange sights he has seen.

Then a whaling cruise begins, carrying the crew into the frozen seas of the far north. Ballantyne builds the story around ice, cold, and the daily work of a whale ship. Buzzby's grit and dry talk hold the tale together. It is one of the books that made Ballantyne's name for sea and ice adventure.
21852-folklore-as-an-historical-science:
Old tales and customs are treated as real evidence of the past in George Laurence Gomme's Folklore as an Historical Science, first published in 1908. Gomme argues that folk tales, local traditions, and even traditional law preserve facts that written history missed. His frontispiece shows the Pedlar's Seat in Swaffham Church, tied to the old Pedlar of Swaffham legend. Carved figures of the pedlar and his dog back the argument in wood.

Later chapters set out materials and methods, then the mental and social conditions behind tradition. Totem customs in Australia and their faint survivals in Britain get close study. Gomme writes as a founder of folklore study in England. The book asks historians to take the people's memory seriously, and shows how.
21885-the-ruinous-face:
Helen of Troy's beauty is the wound at the center of Maurice Hewlett's The Ruinous Face, published by Harpers in 1909. Ten years into the siege, most chieftains are dead and the rest are leaden-hearted. Menelaus alone still burns: for Helen, white-bosomed darling of gods and men, and for what he has lost. The corn-lands round Troy have known no plough for a decade.

Hewlett quotes Pausanias on a sanctuary in Rhodes of Helen of the Tree. Famous paintings of Helen, by Leighton and David among them, illustrate the volume. His prose is dense, archaic, and musical, more poem than novel. It retells the oldest love-and-war story in the West through the husband left burning on the plain.
21994-prince-ricardo-of-pantouflia-being:
Prince Ricardo, son of the too-clever Prince Prigio, takes up the fairy gifts in Andrew Lang's sequel of 1893. Lang dedicates it to Guy Campbell, who wanted more of Prigio, the lady Rosalind, and the firedrake. Ricardo finds the fairy presents thrown aside in an old turret chamber: the sword of sharpness, the seven-league boots, and the wishing cap among them. With these he delivers his country from a dreadful red-hot beast, the Firedrake.

Gordon Browne drew the pictures for the Bristol edition. Lang warns new readers that Prigio's own tale explains the family: a king of Pantouflia, fairies at the christening, and one gift too many. Ricardo's adventures teach the advantages of minding one's book, as the dedication jokes. It is Lang inventing fairy tales with a scholar's glee.
22063-the-trail-of-98-a-northland-romanc:
Robert W. Service, the bard of the Yukon, published The Trail of '98, a Northland romance, in 1910. Service had lived the gold rush's aftermath as a bank clerk in Dawson. His narrator opens in bitterness: the banquet of life is spread and the wonder-workers plan their pageants, yet there is no praise in his heart. He has seen, tasted, and tried; ashes and dust are all his gain.

From that confession the tale runs back to the stampede of 1898. The Chilkoot trail, Dawson's saloons, greed, love, and ruin fill the pages. Service's ballads had made the Klondike famous; this novel gave it a full-length story. It remains his one big prose monument to the rush.
22076-the-second-chance:
Nellie L. McClung, the Canadian writer and women's rights campaigner, published The Second Chance as a sequel to Sowing Seeds in Danny. The story returns to the Perkins family on their Manitoba farm. It opens with a shock: steady Martha, the family's rock, has asked her father for two dollars in cash. Thomas Perkins cannot believe his ears, and due bills on the store will not do.

Behind Martha's small request lies a tangle of family hopes and debts. McClung writes about prairie neighbours, courtship, money troubles, and second chances earned the hard way. Her humour is warm and her moral sense firm. The novel shows the prairie West that made McClung famous across Canada.
22079-the-brighton-boys-in-the-radio-ser:
Lieutenant James R. Driscoll wrote The Brighton Boys in the Radio Service in 1918, while the Great War still raged. The Brighton Boys series followed a group of American lads through different branches of wartime service. Radio here means wireless telegraphy, the new nerve system of armies and fleets. The story opens in Philip Burton's telegraph office with a young operator at his key.

Messages, codes, and sudden orders drive the plot. The boys' skill with the wireless set puts them where the danger is thickest. Driscoll mixes real technical detail with the usual series-book escapes. In 1918 such books let boys at home imagine themselves signalling under fire.
22306-human-traits-and-their-social-sign:
Human Traits and Their Social Significance takes up a large question in plain terms. Its chapter on human traits and civilization opens the argument. Two factors, the writer says, have stayed constant through all of history.

One factor is the physical order of the universe, usually called Nature. The other is man's native biological equipment, usually called human nature. Against those constants, people have slowly remade their world to fit their desires. The book weighs what fixed traits mean for society and change. It offers readers an early, clear attempt to link biology, character, and civil life.
22530-from-place-to-place:
From Place to Place, published in 1920 by the George H. Doran Company, collects short stories. One central figure is Tobias Dramm, known as Uncle Tobe. He serves his town in a grim and unusual profession.

Tobe suffers a chronic heart affection that pales his skin. He is neat and prim in his personal habits always. Kind to dumb animals, he is tolerant of small children too. Money matters find him most prudent, saving, almost miserly. Yet an air of loneliness hangs about the old man. By profession, Uncle Tobe is a public hangman. That contrast gives Irvin S. Cobb's tale its pathos. Readers meet a gentle man doing a terrible job.
22565-from-farm-to-fortune-or-nat-nason-:
From Farm to Fortune, dated 1905, tells Nat Nason's strange experience. Nat is a farm boy under a harsh guardian, Abner Balberry. The opening scolding shows Nat's life in a few sharp lines.

Don't talk back, Abner orders the boy roughly at supper. Take your fish to the kitchen, then get to the barnyard. You've got to help me milk tonight, he adds with threat. Don't dare go fishing again without my permission, he finishes. From such a start, Nat's rise makes its Horatio Alger shape. Farm boys in these tales win fortune by grit and luck. Readers get a classic American success story in period dress.
22651-the-unsolved-riddle-of-social-just:
The Unsolved Riddle of Social Justice is Stephen Leacock's short book on the fairness of modern economic life, issued by the John Lane Company in 1920. The catalog record credits the publisher. Leacock, famous as a humorist, wrote here in earnest about wages, prices, and the working day, in the unsettled years after the Great War.

His sample argument chases a circle: shorten hours, and the price of the thing made rises higher still. Even high wages then fail to buy it, since each gain in pay seems only to feed the rise in prices. Leacock refuses easy answers from any camp. The book remains a crisp, readable statement of questions about work and reward that are still argued today.
22684-patent-laws-of-the-republic-of-haw:
Patent Laws of the Republic of Hawaii and Rules of Practice prints the short-lived republic's patent statute and the rules for using it. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. The Republic of Hawaii lasted only from 1894 to annexation in 1898, yet it ran a full legal order, including protection for inventors.

The law requires an inventor to apply in writing to the Minister of the Interior. He must file a description of the invention and of how to make and use it. The terms must be clear, concise, and exact. For a machine, the principle and its application must be explained. Such texts matter to legal historians tracing how American-style patent law spread across the Pacific. The volume is brief, dry, and complete: a working code from a vanished state.
22695-the-comedies-of-terence:
The Comedies of Terence presents the six surviving plays of the Roman comic poet Terence, in an edition sold by Harper and Brothers. The catalog record names no translator and gives no year. Terence, a former slave who became Rome's most polished comic writer, was a school author for centuries, prized for his pure Latin and humane wit.

His plays turn on young lovers, stern fathers, clever slaves, and foundlings restored at the last moment. Generations of students met Latin itself through these comedies, whose lines passed into proverb. The text here closes with the publisher's list of works for sale by all booksellers, a reminder that classics were also merchandise. Readers get Rome's drawing-room comedy in the dress American schools once used.
22743-ruth-fielding-and-the-gypsies-or-t:
Alice B. Emerson wrote Ruth Fielding and the Gypsies, or The Missing Pearl Necklace, a 1915 volume in the long-running Ruth Fielding series for girls. Ruth, an orphan making her way with grit and good humor, was among the most popular series heroines of her day, years before Nancy Drew.

The sample opens at the old Red Mill, where the steady turning of the grinding-stones sets every board and beam a-quiver. The air hangs full of grain dust and fine stone dust. Around that mill, a missing pearl necklace and a band of Gypsies set the mystery in motion. Emerson writes brisk, wholesome adventure, with Ruth's friendships carrying as much weight as the plot. The book preserves girls' series fiction in its classic form.
22754-masters-of-space:
Masters of Space is a science fiction novel of the United States space navy and a mysterious alien power in deep space. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its officers talk pure service. Captain Sawtelle is old-school Navy brass who goes strictly by the book. A junior named Jarve is warned to keep on his own side of the line.

Karns insists the line be drawn razor-sharp, just where the Advisory Board's directive places it. Next time the captain crosses it, he says, kick his face in. Such counsel promises mutiny-grade friction aboard ship. Alien masters, human pride, and naval discipline collide in the pulp manner. The book is space opera with its boots in the wardroom.
22928-sacrifice:
Stephen French Whitman's Sacrifice, published in 1922, follows a wealthy woman through the pleasure routes of Europe. Wealth, the narrator notes, neutralized every hardship of her journeys. Even her money could not buy calm seas on every crossing, or clear skies over the Riviera on every visit. In Venice at midnight, gondoliers' soft, hoarse cries made her toss on her canopied bed.

Restlessness inside luxury drives the novel. Whitman sets his heroine's unease against hotels, trains, and bright coasts, asking what her comfort costs and what it hides. The title promises a price to be paid. Readers get a polished postwar society novel, observant about money and manners, with travel writing woven through its scenes.
23128-the-king-s-esquires-or-the-jewel-o:
A youth paces at Fontainebleau in The King's Esquires, or The Jewel of France. In a duty room adjoining the king's private apartments, a youth on the edge of manhood paces without rest. Now and then he glances from the low window across the Fontainebleau forest, where kings once loved to hunt.

George Manville Fenn, to whom this tale is credited, sets his esquires in the France of Francis the First, where a jewel draws boys into court intrigue. Pageantry, duels, and forest rides fill the chapters in Fenn's practiced manner. He wrote dozens of such historical adventures for boys. The Fontainebleau opening does his scene-setting in one window, a restless boy, a hunting forest, and centuries of kings behind the glass.
23153-the-big-bounce:
Walter S. Tevis tinkers in a chem lab in The Big Bounce. The narrator's project sounds modest. He wants a better eraser, one that soaks up graphite without wearing the paper. His other drafting inventions, a dimensional curve and photosensitive ink, already worked quite well.

An eraser that absorbs graphite without wear sounds harmless, until the bounce of the title arrives. Tevis, later famous for The Hustler and The Man Who Fell to Earth, began in the science-fiction magazines with inventions like this one. Small discovery, large consequences, told dry. The drafting-table setting keeps the wonder grounded in shop talk. Readers meet a major talent at the workbench, early and already exact.
23230-boys-their-work-and-influence:
Boys: Their Work and Influence is a book of guidance for boys, about conduct at home and beyond. Its advice is direct and practical. A boy should not be a bully, either to his brothers or his sisters. He should not be selfish, or claim all he can for himself.

Share and share alike, the book insists, should be the rule. Gentleness toward girls and little ones is pressed as a duty, not a favour. Even teasing a sister when they are left alone is named as a fault to avoid. Readers get a clear picture of Victorian ideas about manly kindness.
23266-janet-s-love-and-service:
Janet's Love and Service opens on a town at night, not yet fully asleep. Boyish voices drift from garret to garret across the narrow closes. Late home-comers' footsteps pass below, marked by the watchful ear of the narrator.

The spirit of slumber, the passage says, had not yet taken hold of the place. That wakeful hush sets up Janet's story of love and service. Readers get a period tale of devotion in a close-knit town, where young lives, duty, and affection are watched over by neighbours who miss very little.
23275-the-peasant-and-the-prince:
The Peasant and the Prince opens in the French countryside near Saint-Menehould. Not all the peasants are out on the roads. In the middle of a wood, a little north of the village, a traveller in the lane toward the ponds might hear the sound of a mallet at work.

That lane runs by the grounds of the Count de D—. The hidden worker in the wood gives the tale its quiet opening note. Readers get a story of rank and lowly life in old France. A prince's world and a peasant's world sit one wood apart. A chance meeting can join them.
a-belated-guest-from-literary-friends-an: William Dean Howells welcomes a belated guest to his literary circle. The dean’s warm memoir recalls a late friendship. His gentle pen honors the visitor. A charming piece of literary history, Howells, a memoir.
a-little-tour-in-france: Henry James's 1884 travel sketches of provincial France: Tours, Dijon, and the châteaux, observed with his incomparable eye. Elegant, discerning, and full of atmosphere, it is James the traveler at his best. A classic of travel writing.
a-sicilian-romance: Ann Radcliffe's Sicilian Romance — castles, banditti, and persecuted heroines — helped invent the Gothic novel. Her thrilling mysteries set the pattern for a century. The queen of terror at her best. Trapdoors, veiled nuns, and moonlit castles thrill in her gothic pages.
a-strange-disappearance: Anna Katharine Green's 1880 detective novel, one of the first by a woman in the genre. A young woman vanishes from a New York mansion, and the detective must untangle a web of family secrets. Green, whom Agatha Christie admired, helped invent the American mystery.

In December 2024, the National Security Archive reported that President Gustavo Petro had asked the United States to speed up release of its records on the case.

The request, covered in a posting edited by Michael Evans, rests on a simple fact. American agencies reported on the siege and its aftermath. Their files may answer questions Colombia still argues about, including the fate of people who left the building alive. For readers, the piece shows declassification as live diplomacy between two governments, nearly forty years after the event.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_guatemala_Joint_D:
In November 2019, the National Security Archive joined a public declaration on Guatemala's Historical Archive of the National Police, the AHPN. The statement says plainly that the archive is in trouble: a collection praised across the hemisphere and the world now limps along in a much reduced state.

The AHPN's files document the police role in Guatemala's civil war and have supported prosecutions and family searches for the disappeared. A joint declaration is a defensive weapon; scholars and archivists lend their names to make neglect politically costly. Readers get the text and context of an international attempt to protect evidence of state crimes from slow administrative erasure, a threat less visible than fire or theft but nearly as final.
history-of-france: The History of France, by Charlotte Yonge. The French story. This book preserves that history. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
history-of-the-conflict-between-religion: John William Draper's 1874 history arguing that science and the Catholic Church have been at war for centuries. Hugely influential in its day, it helped create the "conflict thesis" that Andrew Dickson White would popularize. Dated now, but a landmark in the history of ideas.
holiday-romance: Four linked stories Dickens wrote for children, narrated by children themselves in delightfully bossy voices. Weddings, elopements, and nursery politics are treated with complete seriousness, to comic effect. Written in 1868, they show Dickens the father at play, and remain charming reading for the young.
horace: Theodore Martin's Horace introduces the great Roman poet — his odes, satires, and epistles — to English readers. Part of the Ancient Classics series, it wears its learning lightly. A graceful doorway into Latin poetry's most civilized voice. His Sabine farm, his friends, and his mellow wisdom charm every reader.
hypatia-or-new-foes-with-an-old-face: In fifth-century Alexandria, the brilliant philosopher Hypatia teaches astronomy and reason while her city tears itself apart. Christians and pagans clash in the streets, and she is caught between a bishop who wants her silenced and a young monk torn between faith and love. Charles Kingsley's 1853 novel dramatizes the real Hypatia's life and her famous, violent death at the hands of a mob.
ivanhoe-a-romance: Scott's 1819 Ivanhoe sets knights and Saxons against Normans in medieval England. Richard returns. The Tower library holds the full text. It jousted history. Saxons rose. Normans ruled. Romance bloomed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
jack-sheppard-a-romance: Jack Sheppard, a romance, by William Harrison Ainsworth. Another edition. This book preserves that novel. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. The archive guards it with care.
jimgrim-and-allah-s-peace:
Jimgrim and Allah's Peace is an adventure novel by Talbot Mundy, built around a man called Grim. Mundy dedicates it to Jimgrim himself, promising never to print his real name, rank, or honors. The contents list twenty chapters with teasing, quoted titles. The story is told by a journalist sent out from Chicago.

Ordered to Jerusalem in 1920, the narrator lands in a city he knew before the World War. He recalls the bedbugs, the citadel moat, camel prices, and his shaky Arabic. His orders begin with the words, 'Look for a man named Grim.' Chapter titles promise escorts, outlaws, and enemies who prove useful. Mundy mixes spy work, desert politics, and dry humor in his hero's world.
justice:
Justice is John Galsworthy's play of 1910, printed here among his collected plays in the second series. The sample lists the full Galsworthy canon, series by series, from The Silver Box to Windows. Justice stands as number three of the second series, after The Eldest Son and Little Dream. Its subject, announced by the title, is the law itself and what the law does to men.

A young clerk, William Falder, commits a forgery and is ground through trial and prison. Galsworthy follows him from his employers' office to the assizes and into a cell. The play's prison scenes pressed the case against solitary confinement with unusual force. This edition places it among the plays that made Galsworthy's stage reputation.
king-midas-a-romance:
King Midas: A Romance is Upton Sinclair's early novel of 1901, written before his fame. A note explains the book's musical thread. Sinclair built the idea partly on a theme he linked to Beethoven's Appassionata sonata and Fifth Symphony. He admits the claim may be a fancy, but kept it, thinking it too good a story to lose.

Extracts from MacDowell's Woodland Sketches appear at pages 214 and 291. A motto verse speaks of a hero alone, wrestling heaven's fiery gold touch. Part One opens in the merry month of May, as its first words say. The Midas name promises the theme: wealth that turns to a curse in the hands that grab it. This romance shows the young Sinclair before The Jungle made him a muckraker.
lavender-and-old-lace:
Myrtle Reed published her novel Lavender and Old Lace in 1902. Seventeen chapters carry its quiet romance. The first chapter is called The Light in the Window.

A rickety carriage climbs a hill in the opening scene. Its single passenger studies the country with interest and admiration. An attic, a Miss Ainslie, and rumors of the valley follow. Old letters and a garden deepen the mystery and the love story. Reed's gentle tale links a past romance with a new one. Reed's fiction favors kindness over cynicism at every turn. A light in a window becomes the sign of patient love.
letters-from-france:
C. E. W. Bean wrote Letters from France as Australia's war correspondent. Cassell published the book in 1917, with a map and eight plates. A plate shows Australians watching the bombardment of Pozières.

Their mates lay beneath that bombardment at the time, the caption says. Bean reported the Western Front for the Commonwealth of Australia. His letters mix battle detail with soldiers' daily character. He later became Australia's official war historian. These early letters show the reporting that built that reputation. Bean's concern for common soldiers marks every dispatch. Anzac troops trusted him as their own witness.
lost-face:
Lost Face is a book of Jack London's northern tales, first published in 1916. The title story opens in Russian America, where Subienkow's long trail of horror ends. Around it stand six more stories, including 'To Build a Fire' and 'Trust.' All are set in the hard world of the far North.

London writes of cold, hunger, gold, and men pushed past their limits. 'Flush of Gold' and 'The Passing of Marcus O'Brien' add greed and rough justice. 'The Wit of Porportuk' turns on a clever and bitter bargain. The tales are short, stark, and pitiless in London's famous style. They show why his northern stories became classics of adventure writing.
louis-agassiz-his-life-and-correspondenc:
Louis Agassiz: His Life and Correspondence was edited by his widow, Elizabeth Cary Agassiz. She built it from his letters, journals, and family papers. She feared those scattered papers would be lost if not gathered. Her preface says his European years were little known in America, his adopted country.

The book traces a rare life of science with one steady aim. Agassiz rose in Europe as a student of fish and glaciers. He then crossed the Atlantic and became a famed Harvard teacher. Letters in his own words carry much of the story. It remains a warm, full portrait of a great naturalist.
malbone-an-oldport-romance:
Malbone is an Oldport romance by Thomas Wentworth Higginson. A motto from Thoreau's diary asks what Nature is without human life. The contents open with a prelude, an arrival, and place aux dames. Aunt Jane defines her position early and to the rescue late.

Oldport is Higginson's Newport in disguise, of yachts and summer society. Malbone is a charming man with what one chapter calls a multivalve heart. New engagements, dangerous ways, and remonstrances fill the season. Hope's vigil and a storm darken the tale's second half. It ends with a requiem for Malbone himself. Higginson writes with the polish of the genteel tradition.
marie-gourdon-a-romance-of-the-lower-st-:
Marie Gourdon is a romance of the Lower St. Lawrence by Maud Ogilvy. John Lovell and Son published it at Montreal in 1890. Ogilvy dedicated it to Lady Helen Munro-Ferguson, remembering happy days on the river. A French Canadian folk song sounds before the tale.

It opens on a bright August afternoon in the village of Rimouski. The sun shines with a brilliancy Ogilvy calls purely Canadian. Old French Canadian women nod sleepily at their doorsteps. Into this drowsy, beautiful world steps Marie Gourdon. Love and village custom shape her story on the great river. The book preserves a vanished French Canadian summer world.
marietta-a-maid-of-venice:
Marietta, a Maid of Venice, is a novel by F. Marion Crawford. Collier issued it at New York in 1901, in his authorized edition. The scene is Murano, famed for its glass furnaces. Old Angelo Beroviero keeps a Dalmatian waif, called Zorzi, in his service.

The servants distrust Zorzi and call him a likely heretic. Worse, they suspect he loves the master's only daughter, Marietta. Any hundred Murano glass-workers would seem safer matches for her. Yet Angelo keeps the stranger, who knows secrets of the glass. Crawford weaves love, craft pride, and Venetian color together. Marietta stands among his best-loved Italian tales.
mark-rutherford-s-deliverance:
Mark Rutherford's Deliverance continues William Hale White's quiet masterpiece. White wrote as 'Mark Rutherford,' and this text follows a 1913 edition. The narrator settles in new lodgings in Camden Town. He has ten pounds in his pocket and, once again, no outlook.

Chapters take him through newspaper work and new acquaintances. M'Kay and Miss Leroy enter his narrow, thoughtful life. 'Drury Lane Theology' names his wry study of popular religion. Rutherford is a failed minister remaking himself in London. His deliverance comes slowly, through work, love, and honesty. The book is a classic of Victorian religious doubt. Few novels search the conscience so gently and deeply.
martin-conisby-s-vengeance:
Jeffery Farnol published Martin Conisby's Vengeance in 1921. He gave the book to two aunts in a warm note at the front. Chapter heads promise pirates, sea fights, and a long held grudge.

The tale starts when Martin's lone life ends and his troubles begin. A song he knows stirs the past, and hard work fails to save him. He aids a Spanish gent, Don Federigo, then sails into danger aboard the Happy Despatch. A fight in the dark with Pompey stands among the chapter heads. Farnol writes in an old style, with thee and thou in the heads.
marvels-of-modern-science:
Paul Severing wrote Marvels of Modern Science, edited by Theodore Waters. The book came out in 1910, when flight and film were still new. Its chapters tour the fresh feats of the age one by one.

Readers meet flying machines, from Langley to the Wright brothers and Count Zeppelin. Then come wireless, radium, and the work of the Curies. Later chapters tour moving pictures, tall New York buildings, ocean liners, and Luther Burbank's plant work. Each chapter names its key men, dates, and trials in plain heads. Young readers of 1910 could see their own age taking new shape.
masters-of-space:
Walter Kellogg Towers wrote Masters of Space in 1917. Samuel Morse, shown at the front, leads the cast of makers. The book pairs each man with the tool that made him famed.

Morse stands for the telegraph, and Thompson for the cable. Bell stands for the telephone, and Marconi for wireless sending. Carty closes the set with the wireless telephone. Early chapters trace signals from old times through Wheatstone and other forerunners of the wire. First facts on wires and waves come in plain, short heads. Boys of that day could trace each new tool to one man's work.
mercy-philbrick-s-choice:
Helen Hunt Jackson published this novel in 1876. Two long poems about truth and guidance stand before the first chapter. The story then opens on a gray November afternoon in New England. A young man, Stephen White, leans on a gate as the light fails.

The title names Mercy Philbrick and the choice she must make. Jackson builds the tale around conscience, faith, and the claims of love. The opening poems announce the book's moral seriousness in advance. Readers of her later work on injustice will recognize the same earnest voice here. The story keeps its sorrows close to home and heart.
minnie-s-sacrifice:
Frances E. W. Harper wrote this novel of slavery and its aftermath. Harper was born free in Baltimore in 1825 and raised by an activist uncle. She became a lecturer, suffragist, poet, and novelist over a sixty-year career. This rediscovered text was edited by Frances Smith Foster.

The first chapter shows Miriam mourning her daughter Agnes in a lowly cabin. Agnes, enslaved and defenseless, fell victim to her master's power and died young. Harper calls it the old story of slavery's cruelty to women. The novel turns such private grief into an argument against the whole system.
misalliance:
George Bernard Shaw set this comedy in a glass pavilion at a Surrey country house. The house belongs to John Tarleton, who made a fortune from Tarleton's Underwear. His son Johnny is taking his weekly Friday-to-Tuesday visit, novel in hand. The stage directions describe garden games, a portable Turkish bath, and Viennese pottery in flamboyant colors.

Into this comfortable weekend come guests whose marriage plans cross and tangle. Shaw uses the country-house comedy to argue about parents, children, money, and wedlock. The text keeps his spelling without apostrophes, as the editor's note explains. Talk, in this play, is the real action, and nobody escapes undebated.
miss-caprice:
St. George Rathborne published this adventure with his Dr. Jack books behind him in 1893. The first chapter is titled simply Coward. A party of tourists stands on a hill behind Valletta, on the island of Malta. Below them lie two harbors, steep limestone streets, and massive fortifications.

Rathborne pauses to describe Malta as England's second Gibraltar. The Maltese, he says, are a swarthy, robust, fearless people. Against this Mediterranean scene, the tourists' romance and danger unfold. Rathborne wrote dozens of such tales, mixing travel scenery with quick-moving plots for popular readers. The opening cry of Coward sets the tone of honor and danger.
monism-as-connecting-religion-and-scienc:
Ernst Haeckel delivered this address connecting religion and science through monism. J. Gilchrist translated it from the German. Haeckel spoke for a society's seventy-fifth anniversary, answering Professor Schlesinger on scientific articles of faith. He argues that general problems, not narrow specialties, suit such an occasion.

Monism, he says, means one spirit living in all things. The whole knowable world develops under one common law. Organic nature evolved from inorganic nature late, with no sharp line between them. Animal and vegetable, lower animals and man, likewise shade into each other. Haeckel presents this unity as a creed a man of science can profess.
monsieur-maurice:
Amelia B. Edwards published this tale in 1873, told by an old woman remembering her childhood. The narrator was scarce ten years old when the events happened, more than fifty years before. Her father, Johann Ludwig Bernhard of Coblentz, had fought his way up from the ranks in Prussian service. He was wounded seven times and made colonel in 1814.

In 1819 the retired colonel became King's steward of the Château of Augustenburg at Brühl. He fetched his daughter from her strict Lutheran aunt at Nuremberg to live with him. There the child met Monsieur Maurice, the Frenchman of the title. Edwards shapes a child's memories of occupied, postwar Germany into a story of loyalty and pity.
mornings-in-florence:
John Ruskin leads readers through Florence's art in these morning lessons. The first morning is spent at Santa Croce. Giotto, Ruskin insists, is the artist to examine first in Florence. The city, Giotto's birthplace, holds his work of every date and kind, from age twelve to sixty.

Ruskin urges seeing Giotto first in his strong and earnest work. He explains the Franciscan world Giotto painted for, under Dante's advice. A footnote quotes the decree appointing Giotto to build the cathedral campanile, as without superior in the world. Ruskin teaches looking itself: slow, reverent, and exact, picture by picture.
mr-fortescue-an-andean-romance:
William Westall opens this Andean romance far from the Andes, on an Essex village green. Matching Green hosts the Essex Hunt's first meet of the season. The whole village turns out, from the oldest gaffer to the last baby. Huntsmen in scarlet and white breeches crowd the road with four-in-hands and donkey carts.

Tom Cuffe, the huntsman, leads hounds fit to go, while old hands refight historic runs. Westall lingers over the camaraderie of the hunting field. From this most English of scenes, his hero Fortescue's story will travel to South America. The title promises mountains; the opening gives the home the adventurer leaves behind.
my-garden-acquaintance:
James Russell Lowell writes of his garden in this famed nature essay. He starts with White's Natural History of Selborne, a book he loved. White takes readers out of doors on every page, Lowell says. The old parson watched birds and insects with endless calm.

Lowell compares White to Walton in taste and Cowper in kindness. He has walked White's haunts yet still sees them through White's eyes. His own garden at Elmwood gives him the same pleasures. Robins, squirrels, and seasons pass in witty, learned talk. V1 called it a gentle classic of American nature writing from the Atlantic's great age.
my-lady-caprice:
Jeffery Farnol sets this romance among outlaws, oaks, and moon magic. The contents name the Sheriff of Nottingham and desperadoes. A blasted oak and a land of heart's delight follow. The narrator opens while fishing, though he hates the sport.

He fishes because Lisbeth's aunt, Lady Warburton, demands a talk. The aunt fears Lisbeth mistakes friendship for love. Lisbeth is an orphan with one married sister. Farnol writes in a gay, old-fashioned voice of wooing. V1 praised its wit and swordplay in a Regency key. The tale blends Robin Hood airs with a courtship of a willful, charming lady.
my-mark-twain-from-literary-friends-and-:
William Dean Howells recalls his friend Mark Twain in this memoir. They first met in Boston, in James T. Fields's small office. Fields edited The Atlantic Monthly, and Howells was his assistant. In 1869 Howells had reviewed Innocents Abroad with praise and some doubts.

Clemens came in person to thank him for that notice. Their friendship then ran for forty-four full years. Howells praises Twain's broad, free way of speaking. He calls it Southwestern, Lincolnian, and Elizabethan at once. The piece is a warm record of the great friendship of American letters, told by the friend who knew him longest.
nasa-tm-19650013686-instruments-of-space:
G A Vacca, chief of instrumentation in NASA's Office of Advanced Research and Technology, gave this talk in Boston on November 2, 1964. He spoke to the Instrument Society of America. His theme was the instruments of space, the devices that gather data beyond Earth. Such systems serve engineering, science, and medical work alike.

Vacca argues that measuring is what turns curiosity into real research. Only when numbers can be tied to events, he says, can they be understood well. NASA's mission under the 1958 Space Act was to expand human knowledge. Instruments, in his account, are the tools that make that mission possible.
nasa-tm-19650018359-manned-space-flight-:
Goddard Space Flight Center issued this performance analysis on May 14, 1965, for the GT-2 mission. GT-2 was an uncrewed Gemini test flight, launched on January 19, 1965, from Cape Kennedy. The subject is the Manned Space Flight Network, the worldwide chain of tracking and communication stations that followed the flight.

Analysts reviewed how that network performed during the mission. A crewed flight program depends on near-constant contact with its spacecraft. Gaps or errors in tracking affect safety and data return. Reports like this one turned one flight into lessons for the next, as Gemini prepared to carry astronauts.
nasa-tm-19660025135-amtran-hardware-an-e:
Juris Reinfelds, R. N. Seitz, L. H. Wood, and C. A. Ely describe a piece of computing hardware in this May 1966 Marshall Space Flight Center memorandum. The hardware serves AMTRAN, a system meant to make talking to a computer simpler and faster. In 1966, that kind of direct communication was still new.

The device is an electronic interface between people and the machine. It works as an on-line remote terminal for an IBM 1620 computer. The memorandum presents the hardware so engineers could build and use the terminal. Its aim was to speed up the back-and-forth between a user and the computer.
nasa-tm-19670005594-proposed-manned-dyna:
Larry Kiefling, of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama, wrote this proposal on December 5, 1966. Large structures built in orbit bend and shake in ways that are hard to predict on the ground. Kiefling proposes that astronauts do the shaking tests themselves, in space.

He lists the kinds of motion problems such structures are likely to face. His plan calls for tests at each step as a space station is built and grows. He also wants failure study built into space rescue work, plus a test laboratory in orbit. A final section spells out one vibration test in full, meant to judge test gear and methods up there.
nasa-tm-19670020820-a-vacuum-ultraviolet:
Uri Feldman, Marvin Swartz, and Leonard Cohen, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, describe a light source in this June 1967 paper. The source produces vacuum ultraviolet light, which air absorbs and ordinary lamps emit poorly. Growing interest in solar and plasma spectroscopy had created demand for laboratory sources of highly ionized atoms.

Their device is a low inductance three-electrode spark source fed by a high-voltage capacitor. Its main feature is the ability to generate spectra of very high degrees of ionization. A modest spark already produced spectra of highly stripped carbon and iron ions. A stronger spark yielded still higher ionization stages, including iron and argon ions. The introduction contrasts this compact approach with the large hot-plasma machines built at major laboratories. Those new sources, it notes, share complexity and high cost.
nasa-tm-19670029351-on-dynamics-of-two-c:
Frank C. Liu, of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on a futuristic configuration. Two space stations are joined by a long elastic cable. The pair rotates about an axis square to its orbital plane, so the spin supplies artificial gravity inside the stations. Liu analyzes the dynamic problems of that arrangement.

He derives the equations for vibration of the elastic cable and for the angular movements of the two stations. Those motions couple together through the cable's end conditions, a mathematical difficulty he resolves by introducing concentrated fictitious masses. The cable equation is then solved by Galerkin's approach for both free and forced oscillations. A general frequency equation for the system's free vibration follows, and the stations' responses to applied time-varying moments are presented in analytical form. The slack-cable, non-spinning case is explicitly left aside.
nasa-tm-19680016281-hydrogen-standard-wo:
H. E. Peters, T. E. McGunigal, and E. H. Johnson review two years of hydrogen standard work at Goddard Space Flight Center in this 1968 paper. The work, covering January 1966 to April 1968, aimed at field-ready time and frequency standards. Those standards rest on the atomic hydrogen maser, a very precise clock device.

Progress included better thermal control and a large storage bulb maser with an all-metal cavity. State selection grew more efficient, and the radio frequency dissociator design improved. A new digital tuning system needs only a good quartz crystal as reference. Earlier systems needed a second maser for that role. Prototype standards using these features were under construction.
nasa-tm-19680017688-information-processi:
Daniel L. Baty of Ames Research Center asks how task difficulty changes human information processing rate in this study. He used discrete tracking tasks with random inputs. Difficulty was given a firm number value for each task, so tasks could be compared fairly.

Fourteen tasks were tested in all. Nine tasks offered four target choices, and five offered sixteen choices. One-dimensional and two-dimensional tasks were compared at equal difficulty values. The study shows how processing rate depends on the degree of response difficulty. Results like these help designers set realistic demands on pilots and operators. They show how fast people can absorb and act on information.
nasa-tm-19690025535-internal-thrust-and-:
Ali H. Mansour and Richard R. Burley of Lewis Research Center wrote this June 1969 preliminary memorandum, TM X-52621. They measured the internal thrust and pumping performance of an auxiliary inlet ejector nozzle fitted with a clamshell thrust reverser. Ejector nozzles blend extra air into the exhaust to shape thrust across a jet's whole speed range.

Three hardware configurations simulated takeoff, transonic acceleration, and supersonic cruise flight. The clamshell reverser sat fixed at positions matching its working settings in flight. Adding a third air stream improved performance at low pressure ratios, the authors report. Peak thrust efficiency reached about ninety-nine percent at takeoff. It reached slightly higher still in the supersonic cruise configuration.
nasa-tm-19700016141-nuclear-power-for-ma:
H. O. Slone and L. I. Shure of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 meeting on aerospace nuclear uses. It asks how nuclear power would change the design of manned orbiting space stations. Both reactor systems and isotope systems are covered.

The authors discuss what nuclear power would mean for a space station and a larger space base. They compare the main candidate systems against each other. Much of their material comes from NASA's Phase B space station studies then under way. The paper helped planners weigh nuclear power against other ways to run a station.
nasa-tm-19710005528-vertical-tail-loads-:
Jerald M. Jenkins, Ming H. Tang, and George P. E. Pearson of the Flight Research Center in California wrote this report in December 1968. It reports loads measured on the M2-F2 lifting body in its first subsonic flight tests. The M2-F2 was a wingless craft that landed like a glider.

The team measured the forces on the vertical tail during those flights. They also measured hinge moments, the twisting loads on the control surfaces. A lifting body trades wings for a shaped hull, so its tail works hard. Flight data of this kind checked the design math against the sky. It also warned pilots where the craft's controls grew heavy or light.
nasa-tm-19720011311-computer-program-of-:
Charles G Miller III of the Langley Research Center wrote this program report in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2512. High speed wind tunnels and expansion tubes use exotic gas mixtures. Their raw pressure readings mean little until reduced to flow values. Miller's procedures compute the free stream and post shock conditions. The gases covered are carbon dioxide, nitrogen, oxygen, and argon, alone or mixed.

The math includes the effects of molecules breaking apart and ionizing. It assumes the flow rests in chemical balance at each point. The work answered an immediate need at Langley's expansion tube. There, planetary entry studies ran gases like the air of Mars and Venus. A shared program kept every facility reducing data the same way.
naudsonce:
H. Beam Piper wrote Naudsonce as a science fiction story about first contact on a strange planet. It opens with a note on Bishop Berkeley's old question about a falling tree and sound. Piper then asks a new question about sound that science, he says, needs to consider.

Mark Howell lands on a warm planet with soft, mosslike ground and a sweet smell in the air. Major Luis Gofredo, a Marine officer, watches villagers cross the fields toward them. Six men carry a long tube on poles, and no one can tell if it is a cannon. The story turns on how strangers read each other's signs.
newton-forster-or-the-merchant-service:
Frederick Marryat opens Newton Forster with a chapter that jokes about writing itself, before any sea tale starts. He quotes Sterne on the cant of criticism as the most tormenting cant of all. An author, he says, finds the beginning, middle, and end of a novel each hard to please readers with.

The story then follows young Newton Forster into the merchant service, per its subtitle. The record's summary lists impressment into the navy and prison in France for him. A West Indies shipwreck and a post on an East India ship bound for Asia follow. Pirates, treachery, and romance crowd the voyage. Marryat wrote sea life he had lived.
nicolette-a-tale-of-old-provence:
Baroness Orczy published Nicolette in 1922, calling it a tale of old Provence. A list of her books in this copy names Castles in the Air and The First Sir Percy. The League of the Scarlet Pimpernel and Flower o' the Lily stand there too. Her name alone promised romance to her readers.

The sampled pages give the title and author's list, but no opening chapter. The subtitle sets the tale in Provence of an older age. That region of southern France, with its castles and old towns, suits Orczy's taste for bygone courts. Readers who know her Pimpernel books will find her here in a new setting, still in the past she loved.
noteworthy-families-modern-science:
Francis Galton and Edgar Schuster compiled Noteworthy Families, on modern science, as volume one of the Eugenics Record Office publications. John Murray published it in London for the University of London office. Schuster held a Galton fellowship in national eugenics. The subtitle calls the book an index to kinships in near degrees.

The kinships link persons whose achievements are honourable and publicly recorded, per the subtitle. Galton hunted family patterns among notable folk of his day. Such lists fed his wider work on heredity, which later readers judge with great care. The book stands as a record of that project in its own terms: names, degrees of kin, and recorded honours.
o-t-a-danish-romance:
Hans Christian Andersen called O. T. a Danish romance, naming himself as author of the Improvisatore and the Two Baronesses. A Latin motto heads chapter one: quod felix faustumque sit, may it be lucky and of good omen. The narrator then praises a happiness no poet has yet sung.

No lady reader, he says, has felt or ever will feel that happiness. It belongs alone to the male sex, and even then to the elect. The moment is that of becoming a student, of passing the first examination. Cadets, scholars, and apprentices know lesser forms of it, he adds. A young soul first feels its freedom there. The romance grows from that threshold.
off-on-a-comet-a-journey-through-planeta:
Jules Verne wrote the space adventure Off on a Comet. It is also known by the name Hector Servadac. The editor's introduction calls it one of his finest tales. In the story, a comet strikes the Earth twice. It carries off people, land, air, and water.

The travelers tour the solar system on the comet. They return home unhurt after the long voyage. The introduction admits the premise breaks strict science. Verne uses it to teach real facts about planets. Charles Horne edited this edition of Verne's collected works. Ships pass through the great flip unhurt, the notes add. Air and water ride along for the trip as well.
okewood-of-the-secret-service:
Valentine Williams wrote this spy novel about Major Okewood. The contents promise murders, spies, and secret papers. Early chapters name Captain Strangwise and Mr. Mackwayte. Later chapters move to a mill house and a cellar. A chapter is set in Hohenlinden Trench.

The story opens with a shy, quiet clerk at dinner. From there it grows into a wartime spy plot. Williams writes fast scenes in the Buchan manner. The book is vintage spy fiction from the war era. Short chapters and cliff turns keep the plot moving fast. Heads name Nur-el-Din, a white paper pack, and a bridge night. The kit at stake is worth a full hundred thousand pounds.
oliver-wendell-holmes-from-literary-frie:
